screens.title: Intrusion Detection & Prevention Basics
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to detect and prevent many common attacks on Linux servers using tools that are practical for everyday administration. We’ll establish the difference between monitoring and active prevention, show a lightweight prevention tool for stopping brute-force access attempts, and introduce file integrity monitoring so you can detect unauthorized changes. You will also see how regular updates and simple network checks form an essential, complementary layer. As an analogy, think of an intrusion detection system as a security camera that alerts you when something unusual happens, while an intrusion prevention system is like an automatic gate that can close to stop the problem immediately. We’ll ground these ideas with concrete examples: configuring a durable policy for SSH using a jail file, initializing a baseline for file integrity with a tool that stores cryptographic file signatures, and basic commands to inspect network sockets and packet captures. By the end, you’ll understand which tool to reach for, why each measure matters, and how these layers work together to reduce risk on production servers.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Intrusion Detection & Prevention Basics
Intrusion Detection & Prevention Basics
Monitor, block, and verify — practical defenses for Linux servers

This lesson focuses on tools and habits you can apply right away: configure dynamic bans for brute-force attempts, establish file integrity baselines, keep packages patched, and monitor network activity. Each piece reduces risk in a different way: detection finds suspicious behavior, prevention stops it, and file integrity monitoring preserves forensic evidence.

IDS vs IPS, fail2ban setup, aide baseline, updates, basic network checks.
Why it matters
Quick wins protect public services and preserve evidence for incidents.
Who benefits
Sysadmins of public-facing servers and small ops teams that need practical, layered defenses.

Dynamic bans based on log patterns to stop brute-force attempts quickly.

Create and check a cryptographic baseline so you detect unauthorized file changes.
Updates & Monitoring

Layered defenses: detection, prevention, integrity and updates. Use these together rather than relying on one layer alone.

Combine monitoring, active blocking, file integrity checks and timely updates for practical, layered protection.

screens.title: IDS versus IPS — roles and behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the two names you will see often. An intrusion detection system is a monitoring service that inspects traffic or system activity and raises alerts when it sees suspicious patterns. It does not modify system state to stop the activity; instead, it surfaces information for an administrator or automated pipeline to act on. An intrusion prevention system builds on detection by taking automatic actions: it can modify firewall rules or drop connections to block traffic identified as malicious. That difference matters operationally. Detection is less risky because it produces observability without changing traffic, but it requires a response process. Prevention gives immediate mitigation but must be tuned to avoid false positives that cause downtime. A concrete example: a detection-only tool logs repeated SSH failures and sends an alert so you can investigate, while a prevention tool can add a temporary firewall rule to block the attacker’s IP. A common misconception is that prevention always replaces detection. In practice you want both: detection for visibility and forensic trails, and prevention for real-time defense. How will you balance visibility and automated blocking in your environment?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › IDS versus IPS — roles and behaviors
Definition and operational contrast

IDS: Observes and alerts. Keeps a record for analysis and investigation but does not alter traffic.

IPS: Observes and acts. Can insert temporary blocks or drop suspicious packets to stop attacks in real time.

Why both: IDS provides forensic evidence; IPS contains fast-moving threats. Combined they reduce dwell time and aid incident response.

Concrete example
A detection-only tool flags many failed SSH attempts in auth logs. An IPS can add a temporary ban on the offending IP so the attempts stop immediately while you investigate the source and patterns.
Common misconception
Assuming an IPS removes the need for logs. Prevention still needs good logging; otherwise you lose evidence needed for root cause and forensics.
Key Takeaway

Plan for both visibility and automatic response. Tune prevention rules conservatively and keep detection data for investigation.

screens.title: How fail2ban works
screens.narratorSegment: fail2ban is an application-level prevention framework that watches log files for patterns of failed authentication or other suspicious entries and responds by modifying firewall rules to block offending IPs. The process has clear steps: first, fail2ban tails configured logs and uses regex patterns to match failure events. Second, when an IP exceeds the configured retry threshold within the configured observation window, fail2ban triggers a ban action. Third, it updates the host firewall—either iptables, nftables, or firewalld—so that the IP cannot complete new connections for the ban period. Finally, administrators can unban IPs manually or rely on automatic expiry. A concrete scenario is repeated SSH login failures: you configure a jail for the ssh daemon, set the bantime, findtime, and maxretry, and fail2ban will ban IPs that exceed the threshold. A common misconception is that fail2ban replaces a firewall; it does not. It complements existing firewall configuration by dynamically adding temporary rules in response to behavior. How would you set bantime to balance nuisance false positives and real attack mitigation in your environment? How fail2ban works means fail2ban converts observed attack patterns into temporary firewall rules, limiting attack impact while administrators investigate.. In practical terms, from log monitoring to dynamic firewall rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › How fail2ban works
Process steps
1.
Monitor logs: fail2ban tails configured log files and applies pattern matching.
2.
Detect threshold: When failures exceed maxretry in findtime, mark IP for banning.
3.
Ban action: Add a temporary firewall rule via iptables/nftables/firewalld for the configured bantime.
4.
Expire or unban: Remove the temporary rule automatically after bantime or manually by an admin.
Concrete scenario
Multiple failed SSH logins from one IP within ten minutes trigger a temporary ban. You then check the jail status to confirm the block and investigate logs for evidence.
Misconception check
Do not assume fail2ban is a full firewall management tool. It dynamically augments your firewall rules based on observed behavior.
Key Takeaway

Tune detection windows and thresholds so the system blocks real attackers while minimizing accidental bans for legitimate users.

screens.title: Configuring fail2ban safely
screens.narratorSegment: When configuring fail2ban you should avoid editing the packaged configuration directly. The recommended approach is to place your overrides in a local configuration file so updates don’t overwrite your changes. A typical workflow is to copy the shipped file to a local variant and edit the local one. The key parameters you will set are bantime, findtime, and maxretry. Bantime controls how long an offending IP is blocked, findtime is the window within which failures count toward maxretry, and maxretry is the failure threshold. For SSH, enable the sshd jail and point to the SSH log. After editing, restart the service and verify the jail status. A practical example of a small local config snippet is shown on screen for reference. One misconception to avoid is setting extremely long bantime values without accounting for legitimate users behind shared IPs; choose values that reduce attack impact while allowing recovery for accidental lockouts. Always test configuration changes from a separate IP to avoid locking yourself out. Configuring fail2ban safely means use jail.local for overrides; test changes from a different ip and keep ban windows reasonable for shared networks.. In practical terms, use jail.local to override defaults and protect ssh. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Configuring fail2ban safely
Example jail.local snippet
[DEFAULT]
bantime = 1h
findtime = 10m
maxretry = 5

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = ssh
logpath = %(sshd_log)s
backend = systemd
Copy the packaged file to a local file and edit that instead of modifying the default package file.
Checklist
  • Place overrides in jail.local or files under jail.d
  • Set bantime, findtime, maxretry to sensible values
  • Restart the service and validate the jail status
  • Test from a second machine to avoid self-lockout
Operational note
Document your ban durations and unban procedures so the on-call team knows how to respond when a site reaches a threshold.
Pitfall

Very long ban times can block legitimate users behind NAT; consider progressive bans or whitelisting critical IP ranges.

screens.title: Operating and testing fail2ban
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring fail2ban you must restart and verify that it is monitoring the expected jails. Use the system’s service control to restart the daemon and then check the status of the specific jail to see current banned IPs and counters. A good testing approach is to perform simulated failed logins from a separate machine or VM that you control. Attempt authentication failures until the configured threshold is reached and then confirm the ban is present. Check the ban list and firewall rules to ensure the IP is blocked. If you need to continue testing, unban the IP using the appropriate client command so you can iterate. Remember to avoid testing from your primary admin IP; accidental self-bans are a common operational error. A misconception to address is that seeing no bans means the service is inactive—verify that log paths and backends are correct for your distribution, and that fail2ban has permission to read the logs and interact with the firewall. Operating and testing fail2ban means always test configuration changes from a separate ip, confirm bans and firewall changes, and document unban procedures for the team.. In practical terms, restarting, checking status, and simulating bans safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Operating and testing fail2ban
Operational steps
  1. Restart the fail2ban service using your service manager so new settings load.
  2. Query the specific jail status to see tracked IPs and ban counts.
  3. From a separate test machine, perform failed authentication attempts until the ban triggers.
  4. Confirm the ban appears in the jail and in the host firewall rules.
  5. Unban the test IP to continue iterations if needed.
If no bans appear, confirm log paths and whether the configured backend matches your system logging framework.
Testing tip
Always test from an isolated host to avoid locking out important admin addresses. Keep an unbanning command documented for rapid recovery.
Key Takeaway

Testing and verification are essential. Silence may mean misconfiguration, not safety.

screens.title: File Integrity Monitoring with aide
screens.narratorSegment: File Integrity Monitoring is the process of creating a trusted snapshot of important files and directories—including their hashes, permissions, and ownership—and then periodically comparing the live system against that baseline. When a discrepancy occurs you get an alert that a file has changed, been added, or removed. This matters because many attackers modify binaries, configuration files, or scripts to maintain persistence or to hide activity. aide is a widely used Linux tool for FIM. The typical workflow is to install the package, initialize the database to capture the trusted baseline, move the generated database into place, and then run checks on a schedule. You must treat reported changes as actionable evidence: investigate each alert, and only update the baseline after you have verified that the change was legitimate and not a sign of compromise. A common mistake is ignoring aide output or updating the baseline without investigation, which defeats the purpose of monitoring and destroys forensic value. How will you incorporate verification steps into your change management so aide remains useful? content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › File Integrity Monitoring with aide
What FIM captures
  • Cryptographic hashes of files so content changes are detected.
  • Metadata such as permissions, ownership and file size.
  • New, removed or renamed files in monitored paths.
Concrete example
After initializing the baseline, an attacker who edits a startup script will trigger an aide check. The alert directs you to the modified file so you can investigate and preserve evidence.
Misuse warning
Updating the aide baseline without investigation removes evidence. Verify changes before replacing the database.
Key Takeaway

Treat aide alerts as potential evidence. Verify, investigate, then update the baseline only for legitimate changes.

screens.title: Installing and initializing aide
screens.narratorSegment: The practical steps for aide are straightforward but must be followed carefully. First, install the package through your distribution’s package manager. Second, initialize the database so the tool captures the current, trusted state. This will produce a newly generated database file which you move into the active database path. Third, run an initial check to confirm no changes exist against the baseline. After initial setup, schedule regular checks—daily or weekly depending on your change cadence. When aide reports differences, investigate each item. If changes are legitimate, run the update command to generate a new database, review the differences if possible, and then replace the active database with the updated file. A common operational error is running the update immediately without verification; doing so converts potential forensic evidence into the new baseline and hides prior tampering. In a concrete lab, initialize the database on a fresh image, create a small test file to generate an alert, and then follow the verify-and-update workflow to practice the safe response. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Installing and initializing aide
Step-by-step
  1. Install aide with your package manager for the distribution used in the environment.
  2. Initialize the database so aide records the trusted baseline state.
  3. Move the generated database into the active database location so checks use it.
  4. Run an immediate check to confirm no unexpected changes are present.
  5. Schedule regular checks and establish an investigation workflow for alerts.
Example commands (visual reference)
sudo apt install aide
sudo aide --init
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
sudo aide --check
sudo aide --update
Use these as a checklist during setup. Remember not to update the database until you verify any reported changes.
Key Takeaway

Follow initialize, verify, update. Treat alerts as potential evidence until verified.

screens.title: Routine checks and baseline updates
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing file integrity monitoring and prevention tools is only useful when paired with routine operational practices. For aide, run checks on a schedule that matches how frequently you expect legitimate changes—daily for high-change systems, weekly for stable systems. When an alert appears, follow a verification checklist: identify the user or process that made the change, check package manager logs for legitimate updates, and consult your change control records. Only after you confirm the change is authorized should you run the update operation to generate a new baseline, and then replace the active database. For fail2ban and any IPS-like behavior, log and document bans so you can correlate them with other alerts. screens.title: Updates, vulnerability scanning, and what they protect
screens.narratorSegment: Keeping systems updated is the most fundamental intrusion prevention strategy: vendors publish fixes for known vulnerabilities, and applying those updates reduces your exposure to known exploits. Vulnerability scanning complements patching by identifying system components that are outdated or misconfigured and by producing a prioritized list of issues to address. Patching quickly reduces the window of opportunity for attackers, but it must be balanced with testing and rollback plans on critical servers. Scanning without subsequent remediation is of little value; it only produces a checklist. A practical approach is to schedule regular updates on non-critical systems, test updates on staging environments for critical servers, and scan periodically to detect drift or missing patches. A common misconception is that automatic patching alone guarantees security; you still need testing, monitoring, and verification. For example, a scanned vulnerability may require configuration changes rather than a package update, so treat scanning results as input to a remediation plan. How will you prioritize updates and scans to reduce risk without causing operational outages? Updates, vulnerability scanning, and what they protect means apply patches promptly with testing, and use vulnerability scans to find gaps that need remediation beyond updates.. screens.title: Simple network monitoring for suspicious activity
screens.narratorSegment: Basic network monitoring gives you quick, actionable visibility into services and traffic. Start with socket listings using commands that show listening services and their PIDs; this helps detect unexpected daemons. Use lightweight packet captures to inspect unusual flows when you suspect data exfiltration or unauthorized remote access. For example, capture traffic to an SSH port on a specific interface to see connection attempts and verify sources. Look for unusual patterns: unexpected outbound connections, repeated failed handshakes, or a large volume of traffic to an uncommon destination. Remember that packet captures can be noisy; filter captures to the relevant ports and interfaces to keep them readable. A misconception is that network monitoring alone proves compromise; it provides clues that must be correlated with logs and integrity checks. In practice, combine netstat-like listings, short packet captures, and log correlation to form a reliable incident hypothesis and then act with containment steps if needed. In this lesson you will learn how to detect and prevent many common attacks on Linux servers using tools that are practical for everyday administration. We’ll establish the difference between monitoring and active prevention, show a lightweight prevention tool for stopping brute-force access attempts, and introduce file integrity monitoring so you can detect unauthorized changes. You will also see how regular updates and simple network checks form an essential, complementary layer. As an analogy, think of an intrusion detection system as a security camera that alerts you when something unusual happens, while an intrusion prevention system is like an automatic gate that can close to stop the problem immediately. We’ll ground these ideas with concrete examples: configuring a durable policy for SSH using a jail file, initializing a baseline for file integrity with a tool that stores cryptographic file signatures, and basic commands to inspect network sockets and packet captures. By the end, you’ll understand which tool to reach for, why each measure matters, and how these layers work together to reduce risk on production servers.

These objectives focus on skills you can apply immediately. First, you will be able to differentiate an intrusion detection system from an intrusion prevention system. That means recognizing when a tool only alerts and when it actively blocks traffic, and choosing the right mode for your environment. Second, you will configure and use fail2ban to limit brute-force login attempts; you’ll understand the key configuration options that govern ban duration and thresholds. Third, you will implement file integrity monitoring using aide: initializing a baseline, running checks, and updating the baseline only after verification. Fourth, you will adopt practical habits: regular security updates, periodic vulnerability scanning, and simple network monitoring to detect anomalies. Each objective includes hands-on actions and a reason why it matters: detection exposes suspicious behavior, prevention reduces immediate risk, integrity monitoring preserves evidence, and updates reduce the attack surface. These are complementary skills that together make a measurable improvement in server security.

Now let’s add detail to those objectives so you know exactly what to practice. When differentiating IDS and IPS, practice categorizing a tool by whether it only logs and alerts or whether it can change firewall rules to block an IP. In the fail2ban objective, learn to edit the local jail file safely, set sensible ban windows, and check the jail’s status after a simulated attack. For aide, practice creating a baseline on a fresh system image, run checks to see reported differences, and follow a verification workflow before updating the baseline. For updates and monitoring, build a habit: run the package update command set for your distribution, schedule regular scans, and review simple network listings to confirm only expected services are listening. Why this matters: tools misconfigured or ignored create a false sense of safety. These objectives are practical, repeatable, and directly tied to incident readiness and reducing exposure time.

Start by defining the two names you will see often. An intrusion detection system is a monitoring service that inspects traffic or system activity and raises alerts when it sees suspicious patterns. It does not modify system state to stop the activity; instead, it surfaces information for an administrator or automated pipeline to act on. An intrusion prevention system builds on detection by taking automatic actions: it can modify firewall rules or drop connections to block traffic identified as malicious. That difference matters operationally. Detection is less risky because it produces observability without changing traffic, but it requires a response process. Prevention gives immediate mitigation but must be tuned to avoid false positives that cause downtime. A concrete example: a detection-only tool logs repeated SSH failures and sends an alert so you can investigate, while a prevention tool can add a temporary firewall rule to block the attacker’s IP. A common misconception is that prevention always replaces detection. In practice you want both: detection for visibility and forensic trails, and prevention for real-time defense. How will you balance visibility and automated blocking in your environment?

fail2ban is an application-level prevention framework that watches log files for patterns of failed authentication or other suspicious entries and responds by modifying firewall rules to block offending IPs. The process has clear steps: first, fail2ban tails configured logs and uses regex patterns to match failure events. Second, when an IP exceeds the configured retry threshold within the configured observation window, fail2ban triggers a ban action. Third, it updates the host firewall—either iptables, nftables, or firewalld—so that the IP cannot complete new connections for the ban period. Finally, administrators can unban IPs manually or rely on automatic expiry. A concrete scenario is repeated SSH login failures: you configure a jail for the ssh daemon, set the bantime, findtime, and maxretry, and fail2ban will ban IPs that exceed the threshold. A common misconception is that fail2ban replaces a firewall; it does not. It complements existing firewall configuration by dynamically adding temporary rules in response to behavior. How would you set bantime to balance nuisance false positives and real attack mitigation in your environment? How fail2ban works means fail2ban converts observed attack patterns into temporary firewall rules, limiting attack impact while administrators investigate.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The recommended approach is to place your overrides in a local configuration file so updates don’t overwrite your changes. Bantime controls how long an offending IP is blocked, findtime is the window within which failures count toward maxretry, and maxretry is the failure threshold.
